questions.question: A coil sits in a strong, steady magnetic field. Why is there no induced emf, and what three changes would create one?
questions.solution: Induction needs a CHANGING flux (ε = −dΦ/dt), not a large flux. Any of: change B (move the magnet or vary its strength), change A (stretch/deform the coil), or change θ (rotate the coil in the field) — the three factors inside Φ = BA·cosθ. Steady field, steady flux, zero emf.

questions.question: State Lenz's law and explain why the induced current must OPPOSE the change — what goes wrong physically if it aided it instead?
questions.solution: Lenz: the induced current flows so that its own effect opposes the change causing it. If it aided the change, a tiny push would grow the flux, which would grow the current, which would push more — free energy from nothing, violating conservation. The opposition is exactly the work you must do against magnetic drag, and that work becomes the electrical energy.

questions.question: A bar magnet falls through a horizontal coil. Describe its speed compared with free fall as it approaches, passes and leaves — and why the pattern is symmetric.
questions.solution: Approaching: induced current repels the magnet (like pole facing), so it decelerates below free fall. Leaving: the flux now decreases, the induced current attracts it back — again decelerating. The two oppositions mirror each other, so the retardation is symmetric about the centre. Inside a LONG solenoid with steady flux, it falls freely.

questions.question: Why is self-inductance called the 'electrical inertia' of a circuit, and why does breaking an inductive circuit produce a spark?
questions.solution: Inductance opposes any CHANGE of current (back-emf L·dI/dt), just as mass opposes change of velocity — hence inertia. When the circuit breaks, dI/dt is enormous, so the back-emf L·dI/dt can far exceed the supply voltage, driving a spark across the gap. The energy stored (½LI²) has to go somewhere.

questions.question: Coil A has 500 turns, coil B has 50. Show that M₁₂ = M₂₁ regardless of which coil is the 'driver', and say what M physically measures.
questions.solution: M measures the flux linkage in one coil per ampere in the other (M = NΦ/I). By reciprocity (the same flux geometry links both), M₁₂ = M₂₁ = M for a fixed arrangement — the turns ratio changes each coil's own flux linkage but the coupling coefficient k and geometry set M equally both ways. It depends only on geometry, orientation, turns product and the medium's permeability.

questions.question: Why are transformer cores laminated, yet the same eddy-current effect is used in induction cooktops and magnetic braking?
questions.solution: In a core, eddy currents are pure loss: I²R heating from the changing flux. Laminations break the conducting loops into thin insulated sheets, raising resistance and shrinking the loops — loss falls roughly with thickness². In braking/cooking the heating or drag is the PURPOSE, so a solid conducting plate is exactly what you want. Same physics, opposite engineering goal.

questions.question: In an AC generator, at which coil position is the emf maximum, and why is it zero when the coil is perpendicular to the field?
questions.solution: Flux Φ = BA·cosθ; emf ε = −dΦ/dt = BAω·sinθ. Maximum emf occurs when the coil plane is PARALLEL to B (θ = 0 or π: flux is maximum but changing fastest). When the coil plane is perpendicular to B (θ = π/2), flux is momentarily at its extreme (maximum magnitude) with zero rate of change — hence zero emf. Maximum flux ≠ maximum emf; that inversion is the tested point.

questions.question: Why does a transformer work for AC but not for a steady DC supply, even at the same voltage?
questions.solution: The secondary emf is proportional to dΦ/dt. AC constantly changes the flux (ε₂ ∝ frequency), so power transfers. Steady DC gives constant flux — dΦ/dt = 0, no secondary emf. Worse, DC sees only the tiny primary resistance, so the primary draws a destructive current. 'Transformer = flux-changer' is the one-line principle.
